title: Adjectives - Types and Degrees of Comparison

questions.question: Which type of Adjective is 'Indian' in the phrase 'Indian seas'?
questions.rationale: 'Indian' is a Proper Adjective — it is derived from the Proper Noun 'India'.

questions.question: What is the Comparative Degree of 'Rich'?
questions.rationale: The Comparative Degree of 'Rich' is 'Richer', followed by 'Richest' as the Superlative Degree.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly avoids a double comparative?
options: He is more faster than his brother.
He is faster than his brother.
He is more wiser than her.
He is more taller than me.
questions.rationale: Double comparatives like 'more faster' or 'more wiser' are incorrect — the rule states to never combine 'more' with an '-er' comparative.

questions.question: In the comparative structure "He is wiser than any other boy in his class", what must follow 'any other'?
questions.rationale: The structure 'Than any other' is followed by a Singular Noun, as in 'any other boy'.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly applies the rule for the Superlative Degree (Rule 3)?
options: He is wisest boy in the class.
He is the wisest boy in the class.
He is a wisest boy in the class.
He is more wise boy in the class.
questions.rationale: The Superlative Degree always takes the article 'the' before it — e.g., 'He is the wisest boy in the class.'

questions.question: Which sentence follows Rule 4 about verbs of sensation?
options: He seems angrily after the match.
questions.rationale: Verbs of sensation (taste, feel, appear, look, seem, become) take Adjectives, not Adverbs — so 'tastes delicious' is correct and 'tastes deliciously' is wrong.

questions.question: Complete per Rule 2: 'The players of my team are faster than ___ of your team.'
questions.rationale: For plural nouns, relative comparison uses 'Than those of' — 'the players ... are faster than those of your team'; singular nouns take 'than that of'.

questions.question: 'Enough' belongs to which type of adjective?
questions.rationale: Words indicating quantity — much, little, some, enough, sufficient — are Quantitative Adjectives.

questions.question: 'Little' (as in little/a little/the little) is used with which kind of noun?
questions.rationale: Little, A Little, and The Little are used with Uncountable Nouns; Few, A Few, and The Few go with Countable Plural Nouns.

questions.question: In the sentence 'Those mangoes are ripe.', 'Those' is which type of adjective?
questions.rationale: This, That, These, Those used before a noun are Demonstrative Adjectives; possessive adjectives are my, our, your, his, her, their.

questions.question: According to Rule 1, the Comparative Degree is followed by 'than' + which case?
questions.rationale: The Comparative Degree is followed by 'than' + Subjective Case, as in 'wiser than any other boy'.
